lessons.title: Lesson 1: Making a simple budget with AI
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Build a one-month budget from rough numbers with an AI assistant.
This lesson builds toward: Given your take-home pay and bills as rough numbers, you will build a one-month budget with an AI assistant, with needs listed first and a small savings line, using no real account numbers.
A budget is a plan for your money: what comes in, and where it goes. It helps you pay what matters first and avoid running out before payday.
Write rough numbers, no account details: "I take home about $1,800 a month. Rent is $700, phone $40, bus pass $60, food about $300. I owe a $50 monthly payment. Help me make a simple monthly budget in a table, with a little savings, and tell me how much is left for other things."
Put needs first: housing, food, transportation to work, phone, and required payments. Then savings, even $10 a week; it adds up and helps with emergencies. Then wants. If the numbers do not work, ask AI: "Where could I cut back?" and decide what is right for you.
Step by step:
- Write your take-home pay and main bills as rough numbers.
- Ask AI for a simple monthly budget table.
- Put needs first, then savings, then wants.
- Ask where you could cut back if it does not balance.
- Save the budget.
Words to know:
- Budget: a plan for how you will use your money each month.
- Take-home pay: the money you actually receive after taxes and deductions.
- Needs and wants: needs are things you must pay for; wants are nice to have.
Try it now: Write your real or estimated take-home pay and five bills as rough numbers. Ask an AI assistant to make a simple monthly budget table with a small savings line.
You can now make a simple monthly budget with AI help, without sharing private details.

options: What you receive after taxes and deductions
check.why: Take-home pay is the money you actually receive to budget with.

check.q: You want AI to help with a budget. What would you type?
check.why: Rough amounts are enough, and private numbers stay out of AI.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Tracking spending and bills
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Track what you spend for a week and set reminders for bill due dates.
This lesson builds toward: Using a note and your phone's reminders, you will track your spending for a week and set a reminder for each bill's due date, with each reminder set a few days before the due date.
A budget only works if you know where money actually goes. For one week, write down everything you spend in a note on your phone: the item and the amount. Small things like snacks and rideshares add up.
At the end of the week, paste the list (no card numbers) into AI and ask: "Group my spending into categories and total each one. Where did most of my money go?"
Late fees waste money. Set a phone reminder a few days before each bill is due: "Remind me to pay my phone bill on the 12th of every month." Pay bills only through the company's official app or website, or in person.
Step by step:
- Write every purchase in a phone note for one week.
- Ask AI to group and total it.
- Compare with your budget.
- Set a monthly reminder before each bill's due date.
- Pay only through official apps, websites or in person.
Words to know:
- Category: a group of similar spending, like food or transportation.
- Late fee: extra money charged when a bill is paid after its due date.
- Due date: the last day to pay a bill on time.
Try it now: Start a spending note today. Then set a repeating monthly reminder for one bill a few days before it is due.
You can now track your spending and set reminders so bills are paid on time.

options: The last day to pay a bill on time
The day a bill is mailed
check.why: A due date is the last day to pay without being late.

check.q: Your phone bill is due on the 15th each month. What would you do?
options: Pay it twice to be safe
Set a repeating reminder a few days before the 15th
check.why: A reminder before the due date helps you avoid late fees.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Safer ways to bank and borrow
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Compare banking and borrowing choices and spot costly or risky ones.
This lesson builds toward: Given banking and borrowing choices, you will compare them and identify costly or risky ones, naming the total to pay back before any loan and spotting upfront-fee scams.
A bank or credit union account is usually cheaper and safer than cashing checks at a check-cashing store, which charges a fee every time. If you had trouble with a bank account in the past, ask banks and credit unions whether they offer "second chance" or low-fee accounts.
Be careful with fast cash. Payday loans, title loans and some cash advance apps can cost far more than you borrow once fees and interest are added. Before borrowing, ask: "What is the total I will pay back, and when?" You can ask AI to explain the terms of an offer in plain words, but not to decide for you.
Scam warning: no real lender asks you to pay a fee upfront in gift cards or by wire transfer. For help with debts, look for a nonprofit credit counselor or legal aid office; avoid companies that promise to erase debt for a big upfront fee.
Step by step:
- Ask banks and credit unions about low-fee or second chance accounts.
- Avoid paying check-cashing fees every payday if you can.
- Before borrowing, ask for the total cost and dates.
- Ask AI to explain terms in plain words.
- Never pay an upfront fee by gift card or wire.
Words to know:
- Credit union: a not-for-profit bank owned by its members.
- Interest: the extra money you pay for borrowing.
- Payday loan: a small, short loan that usually has very high fees.
Official sources:
- FTC: How to avoid a scam (payment red flags)
Try it now: Ask an AI assistant: "Explain in simple words the difference between a credit union, a bank and a check-cashing store, and what questions I should ask before opening an account." Write down three questions to ask.
You can now choose safer ways to bank and spot costly or risky borrowing.

check.q: What is interest on a loan?
options: A free gift from the lender
The extra money you pay for borrowing
A fee for cashing a check
check.why: Interest is what borrowing costs you on top of the amount you borrowed.

check.q: A lender says you must pay a fee in gift cards before getting a loan. What would you do?
options: Walk away; it is a scam
Ask AI to send the gift cards
check.why: Upfront fees paid in gift cards are a sign of a scam.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Checking your credit report for free
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Explain how to get your free credit report and what to look for in it.
This lesson builds toward: Using the official free credit report site, you will explain how to get your free credit report and what to look for in it, planning to request it on a private device and knowing where to report an account you never opened.
A credit report is a record of your borrowing and bills. Landlords, some employers and lenders may look at it. After time away, it may be thin, out of date, or have mistakes, or even accounts someone opened in your name.
You can get your credit reports free from the three nationwide credit bureaus (Equifax, Experian and TransUnion) once a week at AnnualCreditReport.com, the official site. You can also call 1-877-322-8228. Do this on a private device, not a shared computer, because you will enter personal details there, not into AI.
Look for accounts you do not recognize and wrong information. If someone used your identity, go to IdentityTheft.gov for a free recovery plan. You can ask AI to explain credit report words, but never paste your report into it.
Step by step:
- Go to AnnualCreditReport.com on a private device, or call 1-877-322-8228.
- Request reports from all three bureaus.
- Look for accounts you do not recognize and mistakes.
- If your identity was used, go to IdentityTheft.gov.
- Ask AI to explain terms, but never paste the report.
Words to know:
- Credit report: a record of your loans, credit cards and bill payments.
- Credit bureau: a company that keeps credit reports: Equifax, Experian or TransUnion.
Official sources:
- FTC: Free credit reports
- FTC: What to know about identity theft
Try it now: Ask an AI assistant to explain these credit report words in simple terms: "collection account", "hard inquiry" and "payment history". Then write down when you will request your free report on a private device.
You can now get your free credit report and know what to look for.

check.q: Which are the three nationwide credit bureaus?
options: The IRS, the DMV and the courts
Your bank, a credit union and a check-cashing store
check.why: Equifax, Experian and TransUnion are the three nationwide credit bureaus.

check.q: You want AI to help you read your credit report. What would you do?
options: Ask AI only to explain the words you do not understand
Paste the whole report into the AI
Send the report to a stranger online
check.why: AI can explain terms without you sharing your private report.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Planning your week
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Use AI to turn a busy week of appointments, work and errands into a simple plan.
This lesson builds toward: Given a busy week and one money or life goal, you will plan your week and break the goal into weekly steps with AI help, with any schedule conflict fixed and four doable weekly steps.
Coming home can mean many things at once: work shifts, check-ins, job applications, ID offices, family time, maybe classes. A weekly plan keeps them from colliding.
List everything for the week with days and times, in general words. Ask AI: "Here are my work shifts, appointments and errands. Make a simple weekly plan, flag any conflicts, and leave travel time between things." You do not need to say what kind of check-in it is.
Put the fixed things in your phone's calendar with reminders. Leave some free time. If two things clash, call early to reschedule; offices usually respond better to early calls than to no-shows.
Step by step:
- List the week's shifts, appointments and errands in general words.
- Ask AI for a weekly plan with travel time, and to flag conflicts.
- Add fixed items to your calendar with reminders.
- Leave some free time.
- Call early to reschedule any conflicts.
Words to know:
- Conflict: two things scheduled at the same time.
- Calendar: the app on your phone that keeps appointments by date.
Try it now: List your real or practice commitments for next week in general words. Ask AI for a weekly plan with travel time, and fix one conflict it finds.
You can now turn a busy week into a simple plan without conflicts.

check.q: What is a conflict in a schedule?
options: Two things at the same time
check.why: A schedule conflict means two commitments overlap.

check.q: AI's weekly plan shows no travel time between two appointments across town. What would you do?
options: Add travel time and move one if needed
check.why: A real plan needs travel time so you arrive on time.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Turning goals into weekly steps
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Break one money or life goal into small steps for the next four weeks.
This lesson builds toward: Given a busy week and one money or life goal, you will plan your week and break the goal into weekly steps with AI help, with any schedule conflict fixed and four doable weekly steps.
Big goals, like saving for a deposit on an apartment, getting a driver's license, or paying down a debt, can feel far away. Breaking them into weekly steps makes them doable.
Ask AI: "My goal is to save $600 for an apartment deposit in four months. I take home about $1,800 a month. Break it into weekly steps and small actions." Or: "Help me plan the steps to get my driver's license back in my state. Tell me what to check with the DMV."
Pick one goal, write the four weekly steps, and put the first one in your calendar. Check in each week: what did I do, what is next? For legal steps such as license reinstatement, fines or record questions, confirm with the official office or a legal aid program; AI can only give a starting list.
Step by step:
- Pick one goal.
- Ask AI to break it into weekly steps.
- Write the first four weeks.
- Put week one in your calendar.
- Check in weekly and confirm legal steps with the official office.
Words to know:
- Goal: something you want to achieve.
- Legal aid: free or low-cost legal help for people who qualify.
Try it now: Final task: build your monthly budget with AI from rough numbers, set a reminder for each bill's due date, write down when and how you will get your free credit report, and turn one goal into four weekly steps.
You can now manage your money and your week with AI help, and turn goals into steps you can take.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Monthly budget No budget, or it uses real account numbers or leaves out needs. A one-month budget from rough numbers with needs first and a small savings line. It balances, and the learner asked AI where to cut back if needed. Bill reminders Some bills have no reminder. A reminder for each bill a few days before its due date. Reminders repeat monthly and the learner started a spending note. Credit report plan No plan, or plans to use an unofficial site. Writes down when they will request the free report from the official site on a private device. Also writes what to look for and what to do about an account they never opened. Goal in weekly steps The goal is vague or has no steps. One goal broken into four small weekly steps. Each step has a day and fits around the learner's week. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: How do you make a big goal doable?
options: Wait until you have more time
Do it all in one day
Break it into small weekly steps
check.why: Small weekly steps turn a big goal into something you can start now.

check.q: AI gives you steps to get your driver's license back. What would you do next?
options: Confirm the steps with the DMV or legal aid
check.why: Official offices have the final word on legal steps, so you confirm with them.
